lesson.title: Relative Clause Gym
lesson.subtitle: de man die komt, het boek dat ik lees — choose die or dat

hook.title: Point Back, Then Close
hook.content: A relative clause points back to a noun and then closes with its verb. De man die komt, het boek dat ik lees. The relative pronoun is the hinge.

pattern.title: Die/dat by article, verb final
pattern.content: De-words → die; het-words → dat. Wie for people, wat for an unnamed thing. The relative clause is subordinate, so the finite verb goes last.
pattern.trap_note: Wat is not a universal relative pronoun. Use dat for a het-word and wat only for an unnamed or sentential antecedent.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Relative Clause Gym):
exercises.target_answer: die, dat, wie, wat, waar, wanneer
exercises.meaning: that; which; those, that (conjunction; relative), who, what, where, when
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Relative Clause Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The man who comes is here.”?
options: De man die komt, is hier.
niet De man die komt, is hier.
De man die komt, is hier. (1)
exercises.target_answer: De man die komt, is hier.
exercises.meaning: The man who comes is here.
exercises.explanation: “De man die komt, is hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Relative Clause Gym”.

exercises.idea: The book that I read is good.
cues: The pattern: Die/dat by article, verb final
It means: The book that I read is good.
idea_parts: The book that I read is good.
exercises.target_answer: Het boek dat ik lees, is goed.
exercises.meaning: The book that I read is good.
exercises.explanation: “Het boek dat ik lees, is goed.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Die/dat by article, verb final.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Wat is not a universal relative pronoun. Use dat for a het-word and wat only for an unnamed or sentential antecedent.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Wie is dat?” is word-for-word “Who is that?”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Die/dat by article, verb final.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: Where is the book?
exercises.explanation: “Waar is het boek?” reuses only material taught in “Relative Clause Gym” — Die/dat by article, verb final.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Waar is het boek?” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Die/dat by article, verb final.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “When do you come?”
twist.explanation: Question-word order: wanneer first, finite verb second, subject after it.

summary.outcome: Use die/dat/wie/wat in relative clauses and question-word order in questions.
summary.takeaway: Relative pronouns point back; question words point forward. Both keep the verb in its clause's slot.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The Continuous & Position Verbs.

die.context_phrase: De man die komt, is hier.
die.context_translation: The man who comes is here.
die.etymology_derivation: The de/plural relative pronoun; het takes dat.

dat.etymology_derivation: The neutral demonstrative and conjunction; also the het-relative pronoun.

wie.etymology_derivation: English who is the same question word.

wat.etymology_derivation: English what is the same question word.

waar.etymology_derivation: English where and Dutch waar are the same question word.

wanneer.etymology_derivation: A compound question word; English when is the short cousin.
